# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book teaches university mathematics through one running example: double-entry bookkeeping. Each part takes the same small set of business transactions and describes them again in a new mathematical language. Sets and maps come first, then monoids and groups, vector spaces, graphs, and categories. The main theorems are formalized in Lean 4, so a reader can check them by machine.

The book does not assume any knowledge of bookkeeping. It assumes high-school mathematics.

## Why Part 0 comes first

Before any mathematics, Part 0 shows how the material in this book was found. It treats "the algebra of bookkeeping" as a research topic and walks through the search that produced this book's bibliography: the queries, the databases, the tools that worked, and the tools that failed. Every search reported in Part 0 was carried out on 15 October 2026, and the results describe what the tools returned on that day. Search results change over time, so a reader who repeats a search should expect different numbers.

## A rule this book follows

Every factual claim in this book is checked against a source before it is written down, and a claim that cannot be checked is left out. Bibliographic data was checked against Crossref, arXiv, CiNii Research, Internet Archive catalog records, publishers' pages, or the papers themselves.
